title: Social media engagement with transgender fertility content
screen_reason: BuzzSumo-based content analysis of the 20 most-engaged 'transgender fertility' article links across Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest and Reddit over two 12-month periods. Two physicians graded each link accurate vs misleading/inaccurate against cited research and ASRM guidelines; 25% of links (5/20) were misleading, with per-period figures of 20% and 30%. A quantitative share of items judged inaccurate, with a stated denominator.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language articles found via BuzzSumo; authors based in Las Vegas, United States)
estimates.platform: Article links ranked by engagement on Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest and Reddit (identified via BuzzSumo)
estimates.date: 27 June 2019 - 26 June 2021, analysed as two 12-month windows (27 June 2019-26 June 2020 and 27 June 2020-26 June 2021)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-engaged 'transgender fertility' article links graded misleading or inaccurate
estimates.value_raw: Across both the time periods, 75% of the article links were accurate and 25% misleading (per period: 20% misleading in 2019-2020, 30% in 2020-2021; Table 1 gives 2/10 and 3/10)
estimates.denominator: 20 article links - the top 10 English-language article links with the highest online engagement for the keyword 'transgender fertility' in each of two 12-month periods, identified with BuzzSumo (7,077 total engagements)
estimates.definition: A link entered the numerator if two independent physicians graded it 'misleading or inaccurate': containing both accurate and inaccurate information, commentary that may misinform patients relative to peer-reviewed scientific research, or information inconsistent with ASRM guidelines. The Discussion adds that articles highlighting study findings without noting those studies' limitations were graded misleading
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misleading articles were deﬁned as those containing both accurate and inaccurate information, including commentary that may misinform patients seeking information based on peer-reviewed scientiﬁc research or information inconsistent with the ASRM guidelines."
estimates.source_quote: Across both the time periods, 75% of the article links were accurate and 25% misleading.
estimates.page_loc: p. 102, Results (final paragraph); Table 1 gives the per-period source x accuracy breakdown
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent physicians trained in obstetrics and gynecology (K.V., M.R.) categorized each link as accurate or misleading against the references cited, current research and ASRM guidelines; discrepancies resolved by consultation with the senior author (C.D.), a reproductive endocrinology and infertility physician. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported
estimates.moderator_quote: The social media analytics module BuzzSumo was used to identify the top 10 article links with the highest online engagement using the key words ‘‘transgender fertility.’’ [...] Two independent physicians (K.V. and M.R.) with training in obstetrics and gynecology categorized the article links as accurate or misleading.
estimates.notes: Time series collapsed: the paper's own pooled figure across both 12-month windows (25%) is used as the representative point; the per-period values (20% and 30%) are recorded in value_raw. Top-10-by-engagement truncation -> denom_scope topical + denom_selection curated. Coded CONTENT rather than SHARING because the denominator is a set of 20 ARTICLES (engagement rank only selects them), not a count of share events. borderline=true because the applied 'misleading' label can attach to a wholly accurate article that omits study limitations (an omission/completeness judgement), which pulls toward QUALITY; it is kept as CONTENT because the stated definition requires inaccurate information or ASRM-guideline discordance, which is an external-ground-truth falsity criterion, and breadth is therefore set to the broad 'misleading'. Main quality caveat: n=20 links, a single search term, and BuzzSumo does not track Instagram, TikTok or Snapchat.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) Engagement-weighted share: 'accurate articles accounted for 74% of the total engagements' (Abstract; 7,077 total engagements). This is the ACCURATE side; the misinformation figure (26% of engagements) would be a computed complement, which R8 forbids, and Table 2 / the two-year engagement figure are badly scrambled in this text extraction (interleaved column fragments such as '188 69 / 2,804 1,296 / 774 55'), so no verbatim misleading-engagement total can be read off reliably. This is the paper's only near-SHARING measure and it is lost for that reason. (2) Source-type subgroups (Results, p. 102, and Table 1), all article-count shares reported from the accurate side: scientific peer-reviewed journal 100% accurate (5/5 across both periods), news organization 86% accurate (6/7), alternative media 50% accurate / 50% misleading (4/8). The alternative-media 50% misleading figure IS verbatim and would be extractable as a source-type subgroup, but source type is not the paper's headline denominator and n=8; noted here instead. Caution for an adjudicator: the Results text calls these 'user engagement' percentages, but they reconcile exactly with Table 1's ARTICLE counts (6/7 = 86%, 5/5 = 100%), so they are article shares, not engagement shares - the prose wording is loose. (3) Source-mix shares (alternative media 40% of links, news 35%, journals 25%) are not falsity measures. (4) Platform engagement figures (Facebook mean 56 engagements per link in 2019-2020, 17 in 2020-2021) are volume, not prevalence. (5) Referenced-study characteristics (Table 3, mean impact factor 10.5) are not falsity measures. (6) Country left Global: no locale stated; the only geographic detail is that all but two of the 14 CITED studies were published in the United States, which is a property of the cited literature, not of the content's audience.

rob.design: Cross-sectional analytics-tool content analysis, no human subjects (IRB-exempt, publicly available data). BuzzSumo queried with a single keyword pair ('transgender fertility'), English-language filter, returning the top 10 article links by cross-platform engagement for each of two 12-month windows (27 June 2019-26 June 2020; 27 June 2020-26 June 2021), 20 links and 7,077 engagements in total. Engagement definitions taken from BuzzSumo (Facebook = reactions + comments + shares; Reddit = upvotes + comments; Pinterest and Twitter = shares). Two independent obstetrics/gynecology physicians graded each link accurate vs misleading against the references cited, current research and ASRM guidelines, with the senior author (reproductive endocrinologist) resolving discrepancies. No inter-rater reliability statistic and no coding manual reported. Authors' stated limitations: Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat are not tracked by BuzzSumo; results are most applicable to Facebook; only one search term was used.
rob.item6_quote: Misleading articles were deﬁned as those containing both accurate and inaccurate information, including commentary that may misinform patients seeking information based on peer-reviewed scientiﬁc research or information inconsistent with the ASRM guidelines.
rob.item10_quote: For 2019–2020, 80% of the articles were graded as accurate and 20% as misleading or inaccurate. For 2020–2021, 70% of the articles were graded as accurate and 30% as misleading or inaccurate. Across both the time periods, 75% of the article links were accurate and 25% misleading.
